Amid SIR stir, MeitY asks social media platforms to prioritise govt complaints, label ‘misleading’ content

Platforms have been asked to flag old/archived photographs and videos being presented as current events and content ‘likely to incite violence or other unlawful activity’.

Vrinda Tulsian

08 October, 2026 08:47 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational Image | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on Thursday asked social media platforms to prioritise complaints from “authorised government agencies” about content with “potential implications for public order”. It also directed platforms to “label/contextualise manipulated, synthetically generated or misleading content”.

The advisory was first reported by MediaNama . ThePrint has seen a copy of the document.

Issued by MeitY’s Cyber Laws Division and signed by Joint Secretary Ajit Kumar, the advisory says “false, misleading, manipulated or out-of-context content” is being circulated “in relation to ongoing public events and developments”.

Show Full Article

The advisory does not name the events, but comes amid protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, led by Opposition parties, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and student organisations.

Platforms have been asked to give “particular attention” to “old/archived photographs and videos being presented as current events”, “digitally altered or synthetically generated audio-visual content”, “impersonation of public authorities/persons” and content “likely to incite violence or other unlawful activity”.

The advisory mirrors a Delhi Police post from 26 September, which said a video showing a protest at Jantar Mantar and shared by accounts including Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut was “archived material from a past event”.

Under paragraph 4, intermediaries have been asked to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information, run awareness measures urging users to “verify the authenticity, source and date of information before sharing” and “ensure timely cooperation with law-enforcement”. The list moves from clause (iv) to clause (vi), with no clause (v).

MeitY has sought compliance “with immediate effect” while saying the advisory respects “lawful expression and legitimate public discourse”.

The labelling direction goes beyond the rules MeitY notified in February . The amended Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 limited such labelling to synthetically generated audio, visual or audio-visual content and did not cover text. Thursday’s advisory sets no such limit. It also does not define “authorised government agencies” or explain how “enhanced diligence” differs from the due diligence already required under the IT Rules.

The Centre has previously acted against the CJP online. Its X handle was withheld on 21 May and restored by the Delhi High Court on 7 July after Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said it had been blocked ahead of the 21 June NEET re-test.

Earlier advisories, issued after the Red Fort blast in November 2025 and on obscene content in December 2025, had reminded platforms of the legal consequences of non-compliance. Thursday’s advisory does not specify any such consequences.

Also Read: India steps up AI regulation push with consultation paper likely next month. Deepfakes, safety in focus

The SIR row The protests over the CEC and SIR were launched after a report by The Indian Express on 23 September. The report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders of the Election Commission of India (ECI), saying they had been taken without their knowledge. The objections included changes to Form 6 for new voter registration and the centralisation of the electoral roll database.

The ECI responded that its SIR decisions were taken unanimously.

On 24 September, a day after the report, the CJP gave CEC Gyanesh Kumar 48 hours to resign. On 2 October, Delhi Police imposed prohibitory orders under BNSS Section 163 and shut at least 11 metro stations around Jantar Mantar after the AAP and student organisations gave a call for a protest. More than 500 people, including former Delhi chief minister Atishi, were detained. In Mumbai, Shiv Sena (UBT) leaders Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray led peaceful protests.

On 6 October, INDIA bloc MPs marched to the EC’s office. Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi led the protest and wrote on X, “Gyanesh, it’s done, bro. Time to resign.”

Gyanesh, it’s done, bro.

Time to resign. #IndiaAllianceMarch pic.twitter.com/9ZB6aJfakl

— Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) October 6, 2026

On Thursday, Opposition MPs reached Raj Ghat after being denied permission to protest at Jantar Mantar. They are scheduled to meet President Droupadi Murmu on Friday. The CJP has announced another protest in Delhi on 10 October.

The matter is also before the Supreme Court. On 5 October, the top court declined to suspend the CEC and issued notices to the Centre and the ECI. Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the petitioners, told the bench that interim orders were needed, “otherwise the country will burn”.

The ruling BJP, meanwhile, has said the names of 13 crore voters were not deleted but flagged in the draft roll as dead, absent, shifted or duplicate.

(Edited by Chingkheinganbi Mayengbam)

Trump to honour Musk, Google’s Brin, Nvidia’s Huang with top US science medal

The event, ‘Science: A New Golden Age Summit’, will bring together some of the most influential and well-known figures from the worlds of technology, science and innovation.

Almina Khatoon

08 October, 2026 06:49 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US President Donald Trump | Daniel Heuer | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: US President Donald Trump will award the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk and other prominent technology executives at a science summit on Thursday.

Titled “Science: A New Golden Age Summit,” the event will bring together some of the most influential and well-known figures from the worlds of technology, science and innovation.

Along with Musk, who leads SpaceX and Tesla, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su will also receive the National Medal of Science, according to the White House.

Show Full Article

Dell founder and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will receive the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

“The Trump administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology. These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation,” White House spokesperson Liz Huston told Fox News Digital .

Donald Trump and his donors President Trump will also speak at a White House event focused on scientific discovery on Thursday, according to a social media post by his technology adviser, Michael Kratsios.

The ceremony will be the first time Trump has awarded either the National Medal of Science or the National Medal of Technology and Innovation during his two terms as president.

According to CNBC , Sergey Brin attended Trump’s inauguration and donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Republican National Committee in 2025. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contributed to a fund for Trump’s planned White House ballroom, while Nvidia also donated $1 million toward Trump’s inauguration.

Dell has also been a longtime Trump donor. Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, pledged $6.25 billion to help fund Trump Accounts, a program aimed at helping American children build savings. AMD has also contributed to Trump-related funds.

Trump’s latest financial disclosure shows that he bought or sold shares in SpaceX, Tesla, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD and Google’s parent company, Alphabet, as recently as July.

Also read: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton, the brain behind Apollo 11 flight software, dies at 90

‘Well deserved’ As soon as the news broke, social media reactions poured in. While some users poked fun at Trump for presenting the award and being chosen to speak at a science-focused event, others praised Elon Musk, saying he deserved the recognition and credit for his contributions to technology and innovation.

“It’s a well-deserved honor. For those questioning his credentials, besides his successful @Tesla  and  @SpaceX  achievements, Elon Musk has a B.A. in Physics and a B.S. in Economics from the Wharton School (both degrees from the University Of Pennsylvania)”, reads a comment .

“Trump replaces science with stupidity”, another comment reads.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

3 killed, dozens injured in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh & Abha airport came under fire. Eighty-two military targets were destroyed in retaliation, Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.

Sherif Tarek

08 October, 2026 12:11 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

An air traffic control tower at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Photographer: AFP/Getty Images/ Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

The Iran-backed Houthis struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, killing three people and injuring dozens as the militant group intensifies its attacks on the kingdom while fighting Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, and Abha airport in the southwestern region came under fire on Tuesday and Wednesday, with the two strikes causing damage, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement. The Houthis claimed to have attacked both airports.

A Sudanese man was killed in the assault on the Riyadh airport, according to GACA. Five Saudi nationals, two Egyptians and a Pakistani resident were injured.

Show Full Article

Two women, one Moroccan and one Algerian, were killed in the strike on Abha International Airport, where 28 people, including Saudi citizens, sustained injuries ranging from minor to serious.

GACA said it was working to “assess the damage, verify the safety of the facilities and take the necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and maintain the security and safety of operations within the Kingdom’s civil aviation system.”

In retaliation, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it had destroyed 82 military targets belonging to the Houthis in Saada, Hodeida, Jawf and Marib. These included ballistic missile storage sites and command and control centers, a spokesman for the coalition said in a post on X. Houthi attacks on civilian sites in the kingdom “will not go unpunished,” the spokesman, Turki Al-Malki, said.

The coalition said early Wednesday that it intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh launched by the Houthis and later announced it had destroyed the launch platform used in the attack. The platform was in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, and was being prepared for another strike on Saudi Arabia, the spokesman added.

The assaults on the Saudi airports follow a military campaign launched earlier this week by Yemen’s internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government to “eliminate” the Houthis, a group rooted in northern Yemen. The Yemeni armed forces claimed to have taken control of Red Sea areas.

UK Maritime Trade Operations said separately that a tanker was struck by projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday. It was the first reported strike on a tanker deep within the Persian Gulf in about a month.

The attack comes as tensions between Washington and Tehran heat up again. The White House has asked the Pentagon to draw up military options against Iran that could be executed before the US midterm elections, The Atlantic reported, citing two administration officials. Those backing the attack plan believe it could allow Trump to demonstrate strength and potentially declare some sort of victory ahead of the vote, it said.

The possibility of renewed US strikes on Iran helped push Brent crude up 1.1% to over $101 a barrel.

Houthi Threats

The Houthis, one of Tehran’s main proxy militant groups, took over Sanaa in 2014 and announced a blockade of Saudi ports, claiming the kingdom was besieging parts of Yemen.

Fighting picked up in early September, when the group started firing on Saudi Arabia almost daily and advanced south from their stronghold in northwest Yemen toward the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial strait for energy tankers and container ships. That passage became even more vital after the Iran war endangered ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthi group’s missile threats originate from Sanaa as well as Saada and Amran in the country’s northwestern region, according to the Saudi-led coalition. GACA previously said Jazan and Najran airports were targeted in attacks on Monday, causing damage and injuring three people.

–With assistance from Stephen Stapczynski, Weilun Soon, Jon Herskovitz and Michael Heath.

Pakistan has 48% of the poor in Greater Middle East; poverty in region remains at pre-pandemic levels

World Bank report says the region accounts for 14% of the world’s extreme poor, second only to Sub-Saharan Africa. The increase was driven by rise in poverty in Pakistan.

Debdutta Chakraborty

08 October, 2026 12:07 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational image | Akhtar Soomro | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Pakistan is home to nearly half of the people living on less than $3 a day across the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAAP) region, the World Bank’s Economic Update on the region said Tuesday.

Pakistan accounts for 48 percent of the overall poverty in the region, the report says. This drove the regional increase, which is why MENAAP is the only world region where poverty remains above pre-pandemic levels and is still rising.

Three dollars is 830 Pakistani rupees and Rs 290. Pakistan’s poverty rate rose 6.4 percentage points at the $3.00 line and 3.2 points at the $4.20 line between 2018-19 and 2024-25 and exceeded 20 percent. Poverty rate is the ratio of the population whose income falls below the poverty line.

Show Full Article

Afghanistan, Syria and Yemen accounted for another 47 percent of the region’s population living below the same poverty threshold, according to the report .

Earlier in February, poverty in Pakistan surged to an 11-year high of 29 percent, while income inequality has reached its highest level in 27 years, according to the country’s official statistics.

The World Bank said the region accounted for 14 percent of the world’s extreme poor, second only to Sub-Saharan Africa.

“The increase was driven primarily by a rise in poverty in Pakistan,” the report said, noting that the country’s poverty rate increased by 6.4 percentage points at the $3-a-day line and by 3.2 percentage points at the $4.20 line between 2018-19 and 2024-25.

The bank attributed the deterioration to the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, a macroeconomic crisis characterised by high inflation and currency depreciation, and a prolonged period of economic adjustment that weakened real household incomes and employment opportunities.

The latest estimates show that poverty at the $3-a-day threshold has approached or exceeded 20 percent in Djibouti, Pakistan, Syria and Yemen.

The World Bank then projected Pakistan’s economy to grow 3.8 percent in the current fiscal year, while inflation is expected to reach 8.2 percent. However, once population growth is taken into account, real GDP per capita is projected to rise by only 2.2 percent, compared with 2.1 percent last year.

Also Read: Indians live 2.8 years longer than Pakistanis, says WHO. Here’s why

Shifts through the years The 2024 World Bank update had projected 2.8 percent growth in FY25, 3.2 per cent in FY26, and inflation easing to 9 percent in FY26 for Pakistan and a current account deficit forecast at 0.7 percent of GDP in FY26. For 2025, the MENAAP report put Pakistan’s FY2025-26 growth at 2.6 percent and FY2026-27 at 3.4 percent. The bank has forecast a current account deficit of 0.8 percent of GDP and a fiscal deficit of 3.5 percent this fiscal year. Both are higher than the previous year, but remain within what the report described as manageable levels.

In 2025 the main threat was floods and weak agriculture. In 2026 it is the Gulf conflict, with fuel price jumps, a weaker current account, possible remittance losses, and El Niño exposure.

The World Bank said governments across the region were facing competing demands to protect households from rising prices while also responding to humanitarian needs arising from regional conflicts.

Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the West Asia conflict. Petrol prices increased by 40 per cent or more in Lebanon, Pakistan, Syria and the United Arab Emirates, while diesel prices rose by more than 40 per cent in Pakistan and the West Bank and Gaza.

According to the report, Pakistan sits in the “developing oil importers” group, which is projected to grow 4.3 percent in 2026, while the Gulf economies contract sharply.

Moreover, poorer households spend 35–50 percent of their budgets on food, so higher food and fuel prices hit them hardest. Pakistan is also among the countries where gasoline prices rose 40 percent or more, and diesel is up over 40 percent since the conflict began.

The increases were substantially higher in some other countries, with diesel prices rising by more than 80 percent in Lebanon and nearly 70 percent in the UAE.

Pakistan remains particularly vulnerable as an oil-importing economy. Along with Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Tunisia, it faces the risk of higher inflation and commodity prices, reduced fiscal space, weaker remittance flows from Gulf economies and higher borrowing costs as geopolitical risks persist.

Pakistan’s inflation reached about 11 percent by midyear, according to the report. The fiscal-year forecast of 7.1 percent is however lower than the previous year, and the report projects it rising further to 8.2 percent in FY2027.

In fiscal and external position, Pakistan slips from a surplus to a growing deficit and is listed among the economies facing “significant debt or financing pressures”, alongside Algeria, Djibouti, Iraq, and Morocco.

The report notes that to counter it the government has introduced targeted fuel and farm assistance as it advocates for targeted cash transfers over broad subsidies as cheaper and better for fiscal space.

Then there are remittances. Pakistan is a major labour-sending economy to the Gulf. A prolonged slowdown in Gulf tourism, construction, and hospitality could weaken the income flowing home and remittance decline is named as a risk channel for oil importers generally.

The World Bank reclassified Pakistan, along with Afghanistan, from its South Asia region into a newly created grouping known as MENAAP — Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan in 2025.

Pakistan’s economic and external debt profile increasingly resembled that of MENA economies. Its debt-to-GDP ratio, estimated at around 33.4 percent, is broadly comparable with regional patterns in the region.

Pakistan also shares several demographic and labour-market characteristics with MENA countries, including a high youth dependency ratio, low employment-to-population rates and relatively weak labour-force participation. Female participation in the workforce remains particularly low, mirroring a broader challenge across much of the region.

Pakistan’s economic fortunes are increasingly connected to the Gulf and wider west Asia through remittances, capital flows and energy dependence. These ties have become an important component of Pakistan’s macroeconomic stability, outweighing the country’s relatively limited economic integration with other South Asian economies.

This is an updated version of the report.

(Edited by Nardeep Singh Dahiya)
